paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Hi, everyone. Good to see you. It's been such a long time since I've seen you guys — about a half an hour. It's wonderful to see many of you who are interested in this second course.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So I had an inspiration about six months ago. And for anyone who's new — I don't know all of you — my name's Tim Lowenhaupt. Someone told me I should introduce myself. My name's Tim, and I'm the executive director of the Asian Classics Institute. I've been with ACI in this capacity for about six years, but I've been volunteering and working with ACI since 2010. So it's been quite a while.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I had this inspiration about six months ago — well, actually I've had this inspiration since about 2010, but it all came together just six months ago. And I realized that the Lam Rim that has been being taught — many of you may be familiar, maybe you're not familiar with it. We've had 45 courses. What? We've had 45 courses in the last 14 years.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I realized that there's so much information that we've learned that it would be fun to go back to the beginning and say, look, let's go back and get some of the foundational material again. Let's learn about meditation. Let's learn about emptiness. And let's do this all together — in a relaxed way, not in a 10-day way, not in a deep-retreat way, but just in a relaxed way. Let's talk about the text. Let's talk about what it says, and how do we use it?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Because Lam Rim is not — okay, the 18 courses, if you're familiar with the 18 courses, 36 courses, they're very analytical, if you haven't noticed. They're a distillation — a proper, complete distillation of the Geshe course — that if you were in a monastery studying for 25 years, this would be the primary information that you learn. You learn it in a very analytical way.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: In Lam Rim, depending how you look at it — one way is that Lam Rim is kind of like enlightenment for dummies. The intellectual approach is one way of getting there. The deep study, the homeworks, the quizzes is one way of doing it. And it's a good way, and it's a deep way. It takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of thought, study, homeworks — get it? — quizzes.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Well, Lam Rim is not about that. Lam Rim is about how do we study these great ideas in Buddhism, but in a way that we don't care that it's Buddhism? We don't care whether people become Buddhists or not. In fact, I don't care in my day-to-day life and even in my work. I don't care if people are Buddhists. That's not the point. Yes, you can be Buddhist. Yes, you can do the rituals. Yes, you can do all of those things. And yes, ACI can teach you to do those things.

chapters.title: Lam Rim isn't about making people Buddhist

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And the whole point of Lam Rim is: how do we exemplify the principles of Buddhism in daily life without anyone having to notice that it's Buddhism? And in the class we just taught, we learned about being a bodhisattva — what does a bodhisattva look like? Does a bodhisattva wear a big sign that says "I'm a bodhisattva" and sing it on the street? Do they wear — we talked about a karate belt. I'm going to put on my bodhisattva black belt, so everyone knows that I'm a bodhisattva and they're not. It's ridiculous.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But how do we exemplify the principles in our daily life? How do we live them? How do we come to understand them? And then how do they become relevant for us? But more importantly, how does it allow us — one, for ourselves to have happy, successful lives? How can we reach our short-term goals? How can we reach our long-term goals? And then how can we achieve our spiritual aspirations, all of those things together?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But also, more importantly, the goal of Lam Rim is not — and I repeat, is not — to make people Buddhists. The goal of Lam Rim is that you learn the principles in it. And you don't just learn them and put them in a homework and repeat it and say, "Tim, yay, now I can go to Diamond Way." That's not it. Can you then take those ideas, make them successful for yourself, and then go into a school in Argentina and teach teachers how to lead meditations so their kids can have happy, successful lives?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And you learn the principles so well that you can go into your business, into your office, and be like, "I can help out with this." And you start giving ideas. You start teaching ideas on how to solve business problems without ever saying, "Guess what? Gautama Buddha said this," or "Je Tsongkapa said this," or "my teacher said this." The quickest way to get kicked out of a business meeting, or kicked out of being a consultant, is to say, "Well, my teacher taught me this and I'm going to teach it to you too." They're all going to be like, "Whoa, whoa, whoa. We are a corporate organization and we don't do weird things like that. We don't pray here. We're trying to make a profit."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So the idea is: can you learn these ideas so well that they just become part of who you are? And then people go, "Huh. This person has something. Why does the Diamond Cutter Institute get invited to talk at big corporate events? Why?" Because people go, "There's something in there that could be helpful for us. There's something there." And then you start teaching them the ideas. Maybe you pull out a pen. Maybe you start talking about emptiness. You start talking about an ethical way of life. You start talking about larger questions. But you've learned how to do this in a skillful way, so that you're not saying, "Hey, I learned this in a Lam Rim class that has a lineage of teachers that goes back to Gautama Buddha, and we call it Lam Rim, and blah, blah, blah."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Get the blah, blah out of your head. They're words. They're just words and concepts. Can we take these deep principles, apply them in our life immediately, and then become an example that other people will be like, "What are you doing? I want some of that. What is that?"

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: If you are hanging out with people like we were — where were we? We were in Kyoto. And I just remember we were having fun. We were just being ourselves, having a good time. And you could see people watching us like there's something that those people have that they want. And we weren't being annoying, loud Americans, I just want to point out. First of all, we're a group of multicultural people. And there's a way that we interact with each other, the way we treat each other, the way we treat other people around us, that's completely natural at this point for most of us — except when we're irritated. Because I'm still learning.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: People go, "What is it that you have?" I get it on airplanes, even when I'm by myself. People are like, "What are you doing?" They're just curious. They want to know. And that's a huge part of what Lam Rim teaches us: how to just be a normal person who wants to do extraordinary things — and wants to do extraordinary things in a way that's completely ethical and helps people and doesn't hurt people in the end.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Because you can try to do extraordinary things, but if you're hurting people in it, then it doesn't feel right. And we know this. There's a guilt — at least I have it. Maybe people aren't as empathetic or something, but if I do something that I win and get some good result from, and it hurts somebody else, it just doesn't feel good. There's a part of me that goes, "Ehh." And most of the time, what we do as humans is we just say, "Yeah, whatever," and you move on, and then you take a nap and forget about it. But that's not actually helping people. That's serving number one — that's serving you. If you get something that hurts other people in the process, is the net positivity increasing or decreasing?

chapters.title: Apply it to your life right now

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So what we're trying to do here, and what Lam Rim is — the idea of Lam Rim is that when you listen to a class or you listen to the ideas, how is it immediately applicable right now? You should be thinking that about your life right now. If you're hearing a story about people who — what was it in the chat? Glow of kindness. They have a glow of kindness, and you're like, "I want that." And then you realize that maybe there's times when you don't have that glow, and no one talks to you. No one's looking at you. No one's interested in you. Nobody is interested in a grumpy person, I'm sorry. And most grumpy people are grumpy because they're lonely and they're not connecting with people. So their grumpiness creates more loneliness. Because who wants to talk to a grumpy person?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I don't want to go up to someone who's all negative about life. I'm like, "I've got better things to do than listen to that." Which is also not a bodhisattva thing to do, in parentheses. But it doesn't mean — we go through our natural cycles of happiness and sadness and grumpiness and all those things. And I'm not saying those things aren't real. But on a day-to-day basis, Lam Rim should start making your life better piece by piece, day by day. And yes, we're going to have crappy times, and yes, bad things are going to happen, and I'm sorry that they do — it pains me when they do.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But as I was saying, you should be looking immediately, applying it to your life and being like, "Well, do people look at me that way? Am I an example? Am I a living example?" And I know many of you are. But why do you listen to some people and not other people? Why do some people have the karma to be listened to and some people don't? Why is it that when you get a bunch of Lam Rim practitioners together, the world's like, "Who are these people? What are they doing? I want some of that"? And then you don't go running in and being like, "Yeah, that's Lam Rim." You're like, "Oh, okay." You immediately turn it back and you use skillful means to help them. "What do you need right now? Oh, you're having this problem. What's your problem? Let's talk about it."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I called a friend yesterday because I was having a challenge. I knew what the challenge was, but I was having an emotional moment and I couldn't think. So I called and I said, "I need to blab about this." I knew we would get to the Lam Rim eventually, but I needed the help. And my friend helped me — helped me very dearly, actually — in such a way that I was able to see my own pattern in it, because I'm tired of the pattern. And Lam Rim is also about: what are the patterns that we see that prevent us from becoming that living example?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Because I actually said, in my diatribe — translator's diatribe, my self-loathing monologue — I said out loud, "How can I expect to help other people if I can't help myself?" Those are the words that flew out of my mouth. And my friend took a sip — I could hear her on the phone, taking a sip of her tea, just waiting for the moment to be like, "That's the dumbest thing you've ever said, Tim." I mean, it's true. But it's not true. And it was selfish, and it was self-cherishing. But we were able to get to a place to look at the seeds — what were the patterns going on? What was happening underneath it? And then I was able to move through it. And to me, that's being an example.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I feel like oftentimes we wait to help people because we feel like we don't have the capacity to do it. "I'm not ready yet. I'm not ready to teach yet. I don't know enough ACI. I don't know enough Lam Rim. I'm not successful enough. I haven't run a $250 million company that got sold to Warren Buffett like Geshe Michael. So how could I possibly teach Lam Rim? How could I possibly help other people if I haven't done something extraordinary?"
